Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language designed for readability and rapid development. It features dynamic typing and an elegant syntax (using significant indentation)【2†L101-L109】【10†L480-L488】. Created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, Python emphasizes code clarity and has a rich "batteries-included" standard library【2†L101-L109】【10†L480-L488】. 
# Simple Python example
x = 5
y = 10
print(x + y)  # prints 15

Python supports multiple programming paradigms: object-oriented, procedural, and functional programming【2†L101-L109】【10†L480-L488】. It has automatic memory management (garbage collection) and a fast edit-test-debug cycle (no separate compilation)【2†L112-L119】. The interpreter and libraries are open-source and run on all major platforms【2†L107-L109】. 
# REPL (interactive) example
a = 42
print(type(a))  #

Python is widely used in many fields: - Web Development (e.g., Django, Flask)【2†L101-L109】 - Data Science & Machine Learning (NumPy, Pandas, TensorFlow)【10†L499-L504】 - Automation/Scripting (DevOps, scripts, glue code)【2†L101-L109】 - Education (popular beginner language)【10†L499-L504】 - Software Testing, Game Development, Networking, etc. 
# Example: simple HTTP request using requests library
import requests
resp = requests.get('https://api.example.com/data')
print(resp.status_code)

Python’s concise syntax and dynamic typing make it easy to learn and quick to write【2†L112-L119】. It requires fewer lines of code than many languages (less boilerplate), which improves productivity. A vast ecosystem of libraries and frameworks (accessed via PyPI/pip) enhances its versatility【2†L101-L109】【10†L480-L488】. 
# Python allows swapping without a temp variable
a, b = 5, 10
a, b = b, a  # now a=10, b=5

Python 2.7 reached end-of-life in 2020【11†L0-L4】, so modern projects use Python 3.x. As of 2026, supported versions include Python 3.10 through 3.14【10†L489-L494】 (3.15 is in development). Python 3 introduced many improvements, and code should be written for Python 3.x compatibility. 
# Check your Python version
python3 --version  # e.g., Python 3.10.4

Install Python from python.org or via your system’s package manager. On Windows/macOS, use the installer which adds `python` to PATH. On Linux, use package managers (e.g., `sudo apt install python3 python3-pip`). Ensure `pip` (the package installer) is available after installation. 
# Example (Ubuntu):
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip

Use virtual environments to isolate project dependencies and avoid conflicts. Python’s `venv` module creates a self-contained environment directory with its own Python interpreter【5†L69-L77】. Activate it (`source env/bin/activate` on Unix, `env\Scripts\activate` on Windows) before installing packages. This keeps each project’s libraries separate. 
$ python3 -m venv myenv   # create venv
$ source myenv/bin/activate  # activate on Unix
(myenv) $ pip install requests  # installs in this venv only

`print()` outputs values to the console. It converts all objects to strings and separates multiple items with a space by default. You can customize formatting with `sep` (separator) and `end` (line ending) parameters. 
print("Hello", "World")          # Hello World
print("A", "B", sep='-')        # A-B
print("Line1", end='')            # No newline at end
print("Line2")                   # Output: Line1Line2

`input()` reads a line of text from the user (console) and returns it as a string. Always use `int()` or `float()` to convert numeric input as needed. 
name = input("Name: ")         # User types: Alice
print("Hello, " + name)          # Hello, Alice
age = int(input("Age: "))      # Convert to integer

- Single-line comments begin with `#`. - Multi-line (block) comments can use triple quotes `''' ... '''` or `""" ... """` (often used for docstrings). Docstrings are placed in functions/classes to document behavior. 
# Single-line comment
def func():
    """This is a function docstring"""
    pass  # Inline comment after code

Variables are created at assignment and are dynamically typed (no need to declare type). Common built-in types include `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `list`, etc. 
count = 10         # int
pi = 3.14159       # float
name = "Bob"     # string
flag = True         # boolean

Use `type()` to check a value’s type. Convert types using functions like `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`, etc. 
x = 10
print(type(x))        # 
x = float(x)        # convert to float (10.0)
s = "123"
num = int(s)        # convert string to int (123)

Standard arithmetic operators: - `+` (addition) and `-` (subtraction) - `*` (multiplication) and `/` (floating-point division) - `//` (integer division), `%` (modulo), `**` (exponentiation). The `+` operator also concatenates strings/lists. 
a = 10
b = 3
print(a + b)    # 13
print(a - b)    # 7
print(a * b)    # 30
print(a / b)    # 3.333...
print(a // b)   # 3
print(a % b)    # 1
print(a ** b)   # 1000

Compare values with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. These return Boolean (`True` or `False`). 
x = 5
print(x == 5)    # True
print(x != 5)    # False
print(x > 3)     # True
print(x <= 5)    # True

Combine Boolean expressions: - `and`: True if both sides are True - `or`: True if at least one side is True - `not`: negates a Boolean 
a = True
b = False
print(a and b)  # False
print(a or b)   # True
print(not a)    # False

Operate on integers at the bit level: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift). 
a = 5      # 0b0101
b = 3      # 0b0011
print(a & b)  # 1  (0b0001)
print(a | b)  # 7  (0b0111)
print(a ^ b)  # 6  (0b0110)
print(~a)     # -6 (two's complement)

Iterate over a sequence (list, string, range, etc.). Commonly use `range()` for numerical loops. 
for i in range(5):
    print(i)  # prints 0,1,2,3,4

Repeat as long as a condition is True. 
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1  # countdown (3, 2, 1)

Within loops, use `break` to exit early and `continue` to skip to the next iteration. 
for x in range(10):
    if x == 5:
        break     # stop loop when x==5
    if x % 2 == 0:
        continue  # skip even numbers
    print(x)      # prints odd numbers 1,3

- `enumerate()`: adds an index counter in loops. 
for idx, val in enumerate(["a","b"]):
    print(idx, val)  # (0, 'a'), (1, 'b')
- `zip()`: iterate over multiple sequences in parallel. 
for x, y in zip([1,2],["a","b"]):
    print(x, y)  # (1, 'a'), (2, 'b')
- `range(start, stop, step)`: generates a sequence of numbers, often in loops.

Define functions with `def`. Indentation creates the function body. Use `return` to output a value (default is `None`). 
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name)

result = greet("Alice")  # prints 'Hello, Alice'
print(result)             # None (no return value)

Functions can have positional parameters, default parameters, `*args` (tuple of extra positional args) and `**kwargs` (dict of extra keyword args). 
def demo(a, b=2, *args, **kwargs):
    print(a, b, args, kwargs)

demo(1, 3, 4, 5, x=10, y=20)
# Output: 1 3 (4,5) {'x':10,'y':20}

Variables defined inside a function are local to that function. `global` keyword can reference module-level variables, and `nonlocal` refers to outer function variables. 
x = 10

def foo():
    x = 5         # local x
    print(x)
foo()            # prints 5
print(x)         # prints 10 (global x unchanged)

Use `return` to exit a function and optionally pass back a value (or tuple of values). Without `return`, a function returns `None`. 
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

sum_val = add(3, 4)  # 7

`lambda` creates small anonymous functions. Syntax: `lambda args: expression`. They are useful for short functions used once, e.g., in `map()` or `sorted()`. 
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5))  # 10
nums = [1,2,3]
print(list(map(lambda x: x*x, nums)))  # [1,4,9]

Lists are ordered, mutable sequences. You can index, slice, and change them. Use square brackets to define. 
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.append(4)      # [1,2,3,4]
nums[0] = 10       # [10,2,3,4]
print(nums[1:3])   # [2,3]

Common list methods: `append()`, `extend()`, `insert()`, `pop()`, `remove()`, `sort()`, `reverse()`, etc. 
nums = [3,1,2]
nums.sort()        # [1,2,3]
last = nums.pop()  # last=3, nums=[1,2]
nums.insert(0, 5)  # [5,1,2]

List comprehensions provide a concise way to create lists: `[expr for item in iterable if condition]`. 
squares = [x*x for x in range(1,6)]  # [1,4,9,16,25]
evens = [x for x in range(10) if x%2==0]  # [0,2,4,6,8]

Dictionaries map unique keys to values (unordered, mutable). Keys are typically strings or numbers. Use `{key: value}` syntax. 
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
print(person["name"])  # Alice
person["age"] = 31    # update value
person["city"] = "NY" # add new key

`dict.keys()`, `dict.values()`, `dict.items()` let you iterate through keys, values, or (key,value) pairs. Use `get(key, default)` to safely access values. 
for key, val in person.items():
    print(key, val)
print(person.get("age", 0))  # returns 0 if 'age' not found

Tuples are ordered, immutable sequences. Defined with parentheses or simply commas. 
pt = (3, 5)
pt2 = 1, 2, 3
single = (4,)       # single-element tuple, comma is required

Strings are sequences of characters (immutable). Use single or double quotes. You can index and slice them like lists. 
s = "Hello, World"
print(s[0])    # 'H'
print(s[-1])   # 'd'
print(s[7:12]) # 'World'

Useful string methods: `len()`, concatenation with `+`, and methods like `split()`, `join()`, `strip()`, `upper()`, `find()`, etc. 
text = "Python"
print(text.upper())   # 'PYTHON'
print(text.find("th"))  # 2
words = "a b c".split()  # ['a','b','c']

Use `import module` to include standard or third-party libraries. For example, `import math` or `import random`. You can also use `from module import name` to import specific attributes. 
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))  # 4.0

from math import pi
def area(r):
    return pi * r * r

A package is a folder containing modules and an `__init__.py` file. Use `pip` (Python’s package installer) to add third-party packages from PyPI【5†L126-L133】. 
# Install a package example
pip install requests  # HTTP library

import requests
r = requests.get('https://example.com')
print(r.status_code)

`open(filename, mode, encoding)` opens a file and returns a file object. Common modes: `'r'` (read), `'w'` (write, truncates file), `'a'` (append), `'r+'` (read/write)【19†L323-L328】. 
f = open('data.txt', 'w')
f.write('Hello')
f.close()

f = open('data.txt', 'r')
content = f.read()
f.close()

Use `with open(...) as f:` to automatically handle closing the file, even if errors occur. This is considered best practice for file I/O. 
with open('data.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data)
# File is closed automatically after the block

Handle errors using `try`/`except`. The `finally` block always runs, and `else` runs if no exception occurred. 
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero")
else:
    print("No error")
finally:
    print("Cleanup actions")

Use `raise` to throw exceptions. You can define custom exceptions by subclassing `Exception`. 
def square(x):
    if x < 0:
        raise ValueError("x must be non-negative")
    return x * x

On errors, Python shows a traceback instead of a crash【2†L112-L119】. For step-by-step debugging, use the built-in `pdb` module or IDE debuggers. A quick technique is to insert `print()` statements to inspect values. 
import pdb

def add(a, b):
    pdb.set_trace()  # pause here when debugging
    return a + b

add(1, 2)

For configurable output, use the `logging` module instead of prints. It supports log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR). 
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logging.info("Starting process")

Define classes with `class Name:`. Use an `__init__` method for initialization. Methods take `self` as the first parameter. 
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def greet(self):
        print(f"Hello, I'm {self.name}")

p = Person("Alice")
p.greet()  # Hello, I'm Alice

Create subclasses by specifying parent classes in parentheses. Use `super()` to call base class methods. 
class Student(Person):
    def __init__(self, name, id):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.student_id = id

s = Student("Bob", 123)
s.greet()  # inherits greet() from Person

Prefix attribute names with `_` or `__` for non-public or private conventions. Python mangles `__name` to prevent accidental access. 
class C:
    def __init__(self):
        self._internal = 5   # protected by convention
        self.__hidden = 10   # name-mangled private

obj = C()
print(obj._internal)      # 5
# print(obj.__hidden)     # AttributeError (private)

Different classes can implement the same methods. Python uses duck-typing: it’s the presence of methods/attributes that matters. For example, if multiple classes define `area()`, you can call `shape.area()` on any of them. 
class Shape: pass
class Square(Shape):
    def __init__(self, x): self.x = x
    def area(self): return self.x * self.x
class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, r): self.r = r
    def area(self): return 3.14 * self.r * self.r

shapes = [Square(2), Circle(3)]
for s in shapes:
    print(s.area())  # calculates area depending on class

Decorators wrap functions to modify behavior. Use the `@decorator_name` syntax above a function definition. 
def my_decorator(func):
    def wrapper():
        print("Before call")
        func()
        print("After call")
    return wrapper

@my_decorator
def hello():
    print("Hello")

hello()
# Output:
# Before call
# Hello
# After call

An iterator implements `__iter__()` and `__next__()`. Built-in iterables (lists, strings, etc.) can be looped over. Use `iter()` to get an iterator and `next()` to advance it. 
it = iter([10,20,30])
print(next(it))  # 10
print(next(it))  # 20
print(next(it))  # 30

Generators are functions with `yield` that produce iterators on-the-fly. Each `yield` produces a value and pauses the function’s state. Good for large sequences. 
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
for i in countdown(3):
    print(i)  # 3, 2, 1

`with` statement uses context managers (objects with `__enter__`/`__exit__`). Common use: `with open(...) as f:` ensures files are closed properly, even on errors. 
with open('data.txt') as f:
    data = f.read()

# is equivalent to:
f = open('data.txt')
try:
    data = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()

Use the built-in `re` module for regex matching【24†L139-L147】. Common functions: `re.search()`, `re.match()`, `re.findall()`, `re.sub()`. Patterns are strings; raw strings (`r'...'`) are often used to avoid escaping. 
import re
m = re.search(r'\d+', 'Item 1234')
if m:
    print(m.group())  # '1234'

# Use raw string (r'') for regex patterns

`os`: operating system interface (file/directory operations)【24†L54-L62】. `sys`: system utilities (`sys.argv` for command-line args, `sys.exit()`, etc.)【24†L99-L108】【24†L130-L137】. 
import os, sys
print(os.getcwd())   # prints current directory
print(sys.argv)      # command-line arguments list

`math`: mathematical functions (`sqrt`, `sin`, `log`, etc.)【24†L159-L167】. `random`: random number generation (`randint`, `choice`, `random` etc.)【24†L168-L177】. 
import math, random
print(math.pi, math.e)
print(random.randint(1,6))  # random int 1-6

`datetime`: date and time classes. Use `date.today()`, `datetime.now()`, and format with `strftime`【26†L224-L232】. 
from datetime import date, datetime
print(date.today())
print(datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"))

`collections`: specialized containers (`defaultdict`, `Counter`, `namedtuple`, `deque`, etc.). 
from collections import Counter, deque
data = [1,2,2,3]
c = Counter(data)
print(c)        # Counter({2: 2, 1: 1, 3: 1})
dq = deque([1,2,3])
dq.appendleft(0)
print(dq)       # deque([0,1,2,3])

`itertools`: tools for efficient looping (e.g., `combinations`, `permutations`, `chain`, etc.). 
import itertools
print(list(itertools.combinations([1,2,3], 2)))  # [(1,2),(1,3),(2,3)]
print(list(itertools.chain([1,2], [3,4])))       # [1,2,3,4]

Python has built-in testing tools: `doctest` (tests in docstrings) and `unittest` framework【26†L288-L296】【26†L303-L311】. Writing tests ensures code correctness. 
# doctest example:
def add(x,y):
    """Adds two numbers.
    >>> add(2,3)
    5
    """
    return x+y

import doctest
doctest.testmod()

`pytest` is a popular third-party testing framework (not in stdlib) offering simple syntax and powerful features (fixtures, plugins). 
# pytest example (in a file test_math.py):
def test_add():
    assert 2 + 3 == 5

Use the `timeit` module for timing small code snippets【26†L268-L277】. For full-program profiling, use `cProfile` or `profile` to identify performance bottlenecks. 
import cProfile
cProfile.run('my_function()')  # prints execution time stats

- Prefer built-in functions and libraries (written in C) for speed.
- Use list comprehensions and generator expressions over manual loops when possible.
- Local variables are faster than globals in tight loops.
- Avoid unnecessary data copying; use `itertools` for efficient iteration.

Python uses reference counting plus a cyclic garbage collector for memory management【10†L480-L488】. Large objects (lists, dicts) consume more memory, so delete unnecessary references with `del`. The `gc` module can manually manage cycles if needed.

- The `threading` module provides threads for I/O-bound tasks【29†L129-L138】. Because of the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), only one thread runs Python code at a time in CPython【29†L131-L138】. - For CPU-bound parallelism, use `multiprocessing` or `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor` (separate processes bypass the GIL). 
import threading, multiprocessing

def task():
    print('Running in thread')
th = threading.Thread(target=task)
th.start()

def compute():
    print('Running in process')
p = multiprocessing.Process(target=compute)
p.start()

`asyncio` provides asynchronous I/O with `async def` coroutines and an event loop. It allows concurrency without threads (useful for I/O-bound tasks). 
import asyncio
async def say_hello():
    print('Hello')
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print('World')

asyncio.run(say_hello())

Use `pip` to install packages (`pip install package_name`) and `venv` to isolate projects【5†L69-L77】【5†L126-L133】. Freeze dependencies with `pip freeze > requirements.txt` and install them with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. 
pip install -r requirements.txt  # install project dependencies

Swap two variables in one line: `a, b = b, a`. 
a, b = 1, 2
# swap
a, b = b, a

Use inline conditional (ternary) operator: ` if condition else `. 
x = 5
res = "Even" if x % 2 == 0 else "Odd"  # 'Odd'

Use f-strings (Python 3.6+): prefix string with `f` and embed variables in `{}` for readable formatting. 
name = "Bob"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")  # Hello, Bob!
